transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-26 14:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Alvarez (Redwood AE), Bryan Chu (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (AtlasRetail CTO), Jon Ruiz (Atlas ML Eng), Priya Singh (Atlas DevOps)
Artifacts shared: Redwood benchmark spreadsheet (link), baseline logs (customer), perf deck (shared)

Summary / Topics (auto): benchmark numbers, tuning suggestions, next runs, network/config checks

[00:00] Sofia Alvarez: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this to 45, quick agenda is run through the numbers, talk about any surprises, then next steps. can everyone hear me ok?
[00:12] Maya Patel: yep, loud and clear, thanks.
[00:22] Bryan Chu: thanks, quick note, i'll share screen in a sec, and we've uploaded today's spreadsheet to the drive, link in the chat, it's the redwood-bench-2025-11-26.xlsx.
[00:35] Jon Ruiz: saw it, thanks. quick, uh, initial question - are these runs warm or cold cache? that matters a lot for our chat flows.
[00:45] Sofia Alvarez: good call - these were warm runs except the first baseline set which had cold starts, we annotated that in the sheet. the main set is warmed for both sides but there is some variance on long-context.
[01:02] Maya Patel: ok, can you call out p95 and throughput? those are our primary success metrics.
[01:12] Bryan Chu: sure, flipping to slide 2, so baseline provider (we'll call them ProviderX in the sheet) p95 was around 420 ms for our 1k token chat sim, redwood dedicated, with kv cache and batch size 8, came in at 310 ms p95 so roughly 26% lower p95. p50 improvement is about 18%. throughput wise redwood handled 175 req/s stable vs baseline 95 req/s on the same rig.
[01:46] Jon Ruiz: those are impressive. what's the hardware parity? same GPU types?
[01:55] Bryan Chu: yes, we used the same A100 equivalent nodes per your env description; we matched CPU/mem and network where possible but note the baseline used a generic pack with older cuda libs which might explain a bit of the gap.
[02:12] Priya Singh: were both providers using quant? our baseline was using fp16, i think.
[02:20] Sofia Alvarez: baseline was fp16; our runs used int8 quant with the quant profile we discussed, and we also enabled the runtime kernel selection which picks optimized kernels for the attention path. that's in the methodology tab.
[02:36] Maya Patel: int8 for production is still a question for us - what's the quality delta?
[02:43] Bryan Chu: we ran the eval set, the rouge/accuracy drop is within the threshold you set in the eval spreadsheet, about 0.8% relative on intent detection tasks, and we have a fall back path to fp16 for any failing prompts.
[02:59] Jon Ruiz: there's a mention of KV cache in the notes but some lines show 'KV cash' in the auto transcript, haha, no problem though. can you explain how much the prefix cache helped?
[03:12] Bryan Chu: yes, prefix cache is big for chat — for our sim with repeated system prompts the KV cache reduced redundant compute by about 35% on average and improved p95 by ~40ms. for long-context, the benefit scales.
[03:28] Maya Patel: i see a weird spike at the p99 for some runs - like 1.2s - what's that from?
[03:36] Bryan Chu: we dug in, those tail spikes correlate to occasional GC events in the baseline provider's runtime and some network retries. in our runs the p99 was 520-700ms depending on the run, most tails are from cold starts or big context windows.
[03:52] Jon Ruiz: do you have the raw logs for the tail traces?
[03:57] Sofia Alvarez: yes, uploaded the raw trace bundle - link in the sheet, under raw_logs/p99_traces.
[04:05] Priya Singh: from infra side, any notable egress or bandwidth differences? we saw one note about higher egress on the baseline side.
[04:13] Bryan Chu: we measured network transfer per request; redwood's runtime sends same token payloads but because of batching differences the baseline did more smaller RPCs which increased overhead. net egress was similar in bytes but more chattier.
[04:30] Maya Patel: on throughput we saw some variability when we pushed synthetic traffic to 250 rps, redwood dropped to 210 then stabilized, baseline errored earlier. is that correct?
[04:40] Bryan Chu: yes, for 250 rps the baseline hit resource contention and retries; we configured Redwood dedicated with burst headroom and autoscale settings so it smoothed out to 210 then the autoscaler added a node to keep it stable.
[04:55] Sofia Alvarez: one nuance — our default batching can add a few ms for p50 but gives much better throughput; we can tune batching to meet your p95 SLO.
[05:06] Jon Ruiz: what's the smallest batch we'd reasonably run to not lose the throughput benefits?
[05:12] Bryan Chu: for your workload, batch 4 is a sweet spot in our tests; batch 2 lowers p50 but halves throughput compared to batch 8. we'll share recommended tradeoff curves in the spreadsheet.
[05:25] Maya Patel: any differences in latency for long-context 8k token prompts? we have some customers hitting 6-8k regularly.
[05:33] Bryan Chu: long-context runs show smaller relative gains due to memory and kv lookup times, but with optimized kernels and streaming we saw 15% lower p95 and 1.4x throughput vs baseline for 8k tests when using the int8+kv profile. one caveat: quant profile tuning matters more at those sizes.
[05:52] Jon Ruiz: ok, can you explain the quant profile a bit - is it a one-click option or do you need special build?
[05:59] Bryan Chu: it's a runtime profile we apply during compilation stage - no custom build needed for Dedicated, it's a config + model compile step. for Private infra there are additional steps but similar flow.
[06:12] Maya Patel: about security, did we run with customer keys / KMS? any perf impact for encryption at rest?
[06:20] Sofia Alvarez: for the POC we used customer-managed keys for model encryption at rest; KMS calls are asynchronous and we measured negligible perf impact on inference paths. those details are in the security_notes tab.
[06:35] Priya Singh: great. for the next run we want to test a warmed baseline with same quant settings, is that feasible?
[06:41] Sofia Alvarez: yes, jon you mentioned you'd run a warmed baseline run. that will be helpful to isolate infra differences.
[06:49] Jon Ruiz: yep i'll do that, likely early next week.
[06:54] Maya Patel: one more point — cost per 1M tokens was discussed earlier, how did Redwood compare?
[07:02] Bryan Chu: cost depends on util and batching; on our numbers Redwood's cost-per-token for this workload was about 18% lower due to higher utilization and int8 memory savings; we'll provide a cost breakdown per route in the sheet.
[07:18] Sofia Alvarez: question from chat - any issues with SSO/SAML during the dedicated test?
[07:23] Priya Singh: we did hit an SSO redirect quirk once but that's on our side, not Redwood.
[07:28] Bryan Chu: noted, we can help debug if you want, but not required for now.
[07:33] Maya Patel: ok, next steps recap?
[07:36] Sofia Alvarez: recapping - Sofia send full spreadsheet + raw logs (by 11/28), Jon to re-run baseline warmed (by 12/01), Bryan to propose batch/quant tuning and run one more warmed run from our side with those settings (by 11/30), Priya to validate VPC rules (by 11/29).
[07:52] Jon Ruiz: one operational question - if we go to dedicated, how fast is autoscale adding nodes? we need to know warmup time.
[07:59] Bryan Chu: autoscale adds in minutes - default cold start to effective capacity was about 3-5 min in our tests, we also support burst reserved headroom to eliminate scaling latency.
[08:12] Maya Patel: ok that's fine.
[08:18] Sofia Alvarez: any other blockers?
[08:21] Priya Singh: none from infra perspective.
[08:24] Jon Ruiz: none for ML, looks good.
[08:28] Maya Patel: okay thanks everyone, let's get those artifacts and reconvene after the warmed baseline run.
[08:33] Sofia Alvarez: thanks, we'll follow up in email and update the drive.
[08:36] Speaker 1: (end)

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcript had a few mislabels and typos (KV cash, quantisization) corrected in the notes but left raw for traceability.
